section.title: Hagar and Ishmael
section.sectionRationale: God has sworn to give Abram a son, but the years pass and Sarai is barren. Rather than wait, the couple take matters into their own hands through Hagar. The chapter shows the bitter fruit of trying to help God's promise along, and the surprising tenderness of God toward a used and discarded slave woman.
section.thesis: When faith grows tired of waiting, it reaches for its own solutions and reaps grief; yet the God who sees finds the runaway in the desert, hears her affliction, and shows that no one is beneath His notice.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the human scheme that produces conflict and flight; and God's pursuit of Hagar in the wilderness, where she names Him the God who sees.

units.label: The scheme and its bitter fruit

verses.text: Now Abram’s wife Sarai had borne him no children, but she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar.
So Sarai said to Abram, “Look now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her.” And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
So after he had lived in Canaan for ten years, his wife Sarai took her Egyptian maidservant Hagar and gave her to Abram to be his wife.
And he slept with Hagar, and she conceived. But when Hagar realized that she was pregnant, she began to despise her mistress.

Then Sarai said to Abram, “May the wrong done to me be upon you! I delivered my servant into your arms, and ever since she saw that she was pregnant, she has treated me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me.”
“Here,” said Abram, “your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her.” Then Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that she fled from her.

units.label: The God who finds the runaway

verses.text: Now the {{angel|angel}} of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert, the spring along the road to Shur.
“Hagar, servant of Sarai,” he said, “where have you come from, and where are you going?” “I am running away from my mistress Sarai,” she replied.
So the angel of the LORD told her, “Return to your mistress and submit to her authority.”
Then the angel added, “I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count.”
The angel of the LORD proceeded: “Behold, you have conceived and will bear a son. And you shall name him {{ishmael|Ishmael}}, for the LORD has heard your cry of {{affliction|affliction}}.
He will be a wild donkey of a man, and his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him; he will live in hostility toward all his brothers.”
So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: “You are the {{roi|God who sees me}},” for she said, “Here I have seen the One who sees me!”
Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi. It is located between Kadesh and Bered.
And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

angel.gloss: A messenger or angel. The angel of the LORD here speaks as God, promising to multiply Hagar's offspring, and Hagar addresses Him as the LORD Himself. Many read these appearances as the LORD condescending to be seen, a foreshadowing of the incarnation.

ishmael.gloss: The name means God hears. It is a permanent memorial that God heard the cry of a mistreated, foreign slave woman. Every time the name is spoken, it testifies that God attends to the affliction of the lowly.

affliction.gloss: Misery, affliction, hardship. The same word describes Israel's suffering in Egypt, which God also saw and heard. Hagar the Egyptian is treated as Israel would later be treated, and the God who hears Israel already hears her.

roi.gloss: God who sees me, the name Hagar coins for the LORD. She is the only person in Scripture to give God a name, and it is a name born of being noticed in her lowest moment. The well is named the well of the Living One who sees me.

basic.context: God has promised Abram a son, but Sarai is still barren after years of waiting. Following the custom of the day, she gives her slave Hagar to Abram to bear a child on her behalf. The key question is whether God's promise needs our help, or our trust, and what it costs when we stop waiting on Him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a story that describes what happened, not a model to copy; the surrogate arrangement brings only jealousy, cruelty, and flight. The chapter's main point is the character of God, who pursues a despised runaway. Readers debate whether Sarai and Abram sinned or acted reasonably by their culture, but the fruit of the scheme speaks for itself.
basic.originalLanguages: God tells Hagar to name her son Ishmael, which means God hears, because He heard her affliction, the same word used later for Israel's misery in Egypt. In wonder she calls the LORD El-Roi, the God who sees me. Hearing and seeing are the two great mercies of this chapter.
basic.typology: The angel of the LORD who speaks as God and is called the LORD points ahead to the God who comes near and is seen, ultimately in Christ. And God's care for a rejected Gentile slave anticipates the gospel reaching beyond Israel to all the nations.
basic.christ: Jesus is the One who seeks out the despised, the outsider, and the one running away, just as the angel of the LORD sought Hagar. Paul later uses Hagar and Sarah to picture two covenants, the slavery of law-keeping and the freedom of promise fulfilled in Christ, Galatians 4.
basic.god: God is the One who sees and hears those no one else notices. He does not excuse the sin in the household, but neither does He abandon the victim of it. He meets Hagar with a promise and a future.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 4 reads Hagar and Sarah as two covenants. Genesis 21 continues Ishmael's story. Exodus uses the same words of seeing and hearing affliction for Israel in Egypt.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows what happens when faith tries to shortcut God's promise: conflict and heartache. Yet even the detour is met by a God who sees. The true son of promise is still to come, and beyond him, Christ, in whom even outsiders like Hagar find they are seen and heard.

context.literary:
Genesis 16 follows directly on the covenant of chapter 15, and the placement is pointed. God has just sworn that Abram's heir will come 'from your own body,' Genesis 15:4. Chapter 16 opens with the barrenness that makes the promise look impossible, and the first human response to that tension is a plan.

The plan is told in words that deliberately recall Eden. 'Abram listened to the voice of Sarai,' verse 2, echoes Genesis 3:17, 'you have listened to the voice of your wife.' 'Sarai took... and gave her to Abram,' verse 3, echoes Genesis 3:6, 'she took... she also gave some to her husband.' The sequence of taking and giving that brought the first fall is replayed in the household of promise.

The chapter moves in two movements. Verses 1 to 6 happen in Abram's tent and end in flight. Verses 7 to 14 happen by a spring in the wilderness and end in worship. Verses 15 and 16 close the frame with a birth and Abram's age. The first half is full of speech about Hagar; the second is speech to her. Neither Sarai nor Abram ever uses her name. She is 'my maidservant,' 'my servant,' 'your servant,' verses 2, 5 and 6. The first to call her by name is the angel of the LORD: 'Hagar, servant of Sarai,' verse 8.

The angel speaks three times, each introduced with 'the angel of the LORD said,' verses 9, 10 and 11: a command, a promise, and an announcement of birth. The announcement uses a form that recurs in Scripture, the birth oracle: you have conceived, you will bear a son, you shall name him, for a reason. The same shape returns for Isaac, Samson and Jesus.

The chapter is also held together by names. Ishmael, 'God hears,' is given by God; El-Roi, 'the God who sees me,' is given by Hagar; Beer-lahai-roi, the well, carries her testimony into the landscape. Hearing and seeing frame the wilderness scene, and they return in Genesis 21, when God hears the boy and opens Hagar's eyes.
context.historical:
Sarai's plan followed accepted practice in the ancient Near East. Marriage contracts and law collections from the second millennium, including the laws of Hammurabi, make provision for a wife who could not bear children to give her husband a slave woman so that the child would be counted as the wife's. The same laws also anticipate the problem that arose here: a slave who bore a child might claim equality with her mistress, and the mistress had the right to reduce her back to the status of a slave. Genesis 16 shows both the custom and its predictable conflict. Rachel and Leah later use the same arrangement with Bilhah and Zilpah, Genesis 30:3-9.

Hagar is 'an Egyptian maidservant.' She may well have come into the household during the stay in Egypt, when Pharaoh gave Abram 'menservants and maidservants,' Genesis 12:16, though the text does not say so. Her flight is toward home. The spring 'along the road to Shur' lay on the route from southern Canaan toward the Egyptian frontier; the Desert of Shur is where Israel entered the wilderness after crossing the sea, Exodus 15:22, and Genesis 25:18 places Shur 'near the border of Egypt.' The well lies between Kadesh and Bered in the dry south.

The 'ten years' of verse 3 and Abram's age of eighty six in verse 16 set the scene in time. Abram left Haran at seventy five, Genesis 12:4, so the couple had waited a decade in the land.

The description of Ishmael as 'a wild donkey of a man' drew on an animal every herdsman knew: the onager, the wild ass of the steppe, untamed, fast and free. Job 39:5-8 describes it scorning the city and roaming the wilderness. The image foretells a free, independent people of the desert. Genesis 25:12-18 lists Ishmael's twelve sons as princes of tribes settled from Havilah to Shur, and Isaiah 60:7 names two of them, Kedar and Nebaioth, as peoples of the Arabian desert.
context.canonical:
Within Genesis the chapter has a sequel. In Genesis 17 God promises that Sarah herself will bear the heir, while also answering Abraham's prayer for Ishmael: 'I have heard you, and I will surely bless him,' Genesis 17:20, a play on the boy's name. In Genesis 21:8-21 Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, and again God hears the boy and provides water in the wilderness. Genesis 25:12-18 records Ishmael's descendants and ends with the phrase of Genesis 16:12, 'they lived in hostility toward all their brothers.'

The vocabulary of affliction, seeing and hearing runs straight into the exodus. God tells Abram in Genesis 15:13 that his descendants will be 'mistreated,' and in Exodus 1:11-12 the Egyptians 'oppress' Israel, the same root used of Sarai's treatment of Hagar in Genesis 16:6. At the burning bush the LORD says, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out,' Exodus 3:7, and Israel's creed remembers that 'the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction,' Deuteronomy 26:7. What God did for one Egyptian slave woman in Genesis 16, He later does for a nation of Hebrew slaves in Egypt.

The same pattern marks later barren or wronged women. Leah names Reuben because 'The LORD has seen my affliction,' Genesis 29:32; Hannah prays that God will 'look upon the affliction of Your maidservant,' 1 Samuel 1:11; Mary rejoices that God 'has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant,' Luke 1:48.

The angel of the LORD, first mentioned here, appears again at key moments: stopping Abraham's hand, Genesis 22:11-12, in the burning bush, Exodus 3:2-6, and to Gideon and to Samson's parents, Judges 6:22 and 13:21-22. Each time those who meet Him conclude that they have seen God.

In the New Testament Paul reads the chapter in Galatians 4:21-31, using Hagar and Sarah to represent two covenants, one bearing children into slavery and one bearing children of promise, and applying it to believers who were being pressed to live under the law.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see the cost of trying to secure God's promises by human means. Abram and Sarai had the promise in chapter 15, sealed by oath. What they lacked was patience. The narrator does not comment directly on the plan; instead he lets its results speak, and he frames it in the language of Eden so that careful hearers would recognise a familiar pattern of taking what God has not given in the way He has not given it.

He also wanted Israel to notice who suffers most from such schemes. Hagar had no say in the plan; she was 'given' and then left in Sarai's hands, verse 6. Israel, who knew what it was to be slaves in Egypt, were meant to feel the weight of an Egyptian slave being mistreated by a Hebrew mistress, and to remember the law's later commands about treating slaves and foreigners justly, Exodus 22:21.

Above all, the author wanted his hearers to know the character of their God. The angel of the LORD 'found' Hagar, verse 7. He addresses her by name, asks questions that invite her to speak, gives a hard command and a large promise, and names her son after God's hearing. The chapter's climax is her confession: 'You are the God who sees me.' The hearers were to learn that the God of Abraham sees and hears those whom others overlook, even outside the chosen line, and that His purposes for the promise stand even when His people fail.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a practice that was legal in its world, but it does not approve it. The narrator's echoes of Eden and the misery that follows make the point without a lecture. Nothing here authorises surrogacy arrangements, the use of servants for another's ends, or the treatment Sarai gave Hagar. Nor is Abram's passivity, 'Do whatever you want with her,' verse 6, held up as a model of leadership.

The angel's command, 'Return to your mistress and submit to her authority,' verse 9, is addressed to one woman in one situation, and it comes with a promise that guarantees her future and her son's. It should not be turned into a general rule that the abused must always return to their abusers. What carries forward is the revealed character of God: He sees affliction, hears cries, and meets the lowly with dignity and promise. Believers are called to trust His timing rather than force it, and to reflect His care for the vulnerable, James 1:27.

debates.question: Was Sarai and Abram's use of Hagar a sin, or a culturally acceptable act that went wrong?

views.label: A failure of faith
views.case: The plan comes right after God's oath in chapter 15, and the narrator describes it with the words of Genesis 3:6 and 3:17. Sarai blames the LORD for her barrenness, verse 2, and the result is contempt, harshness and flight. Galatians 4:23 calls Ishmael's birth 'according to the flesh' in contrast with the son 'born through the promise.'

views.label: A legal custom used in good faith
views.case: Surrogacy through a slave woman was a recognised solution to barrenness, and God had not yet said that Sarai would be the mother; that comes in Genesis 17:16. On this view the couple may have thought they were cooperating with the promise, and the narrative's criticism falls more on their treatment of Hagar than on the arrangement itself.

debates.bearing: Both views see real sin in the chapter; the question is where it starts. The Eden echoes suggest that the plan itself, not only its aftermath, was a failure to wait on God. Yet the chapter's main interest lies elsewhere, in the God who does not abandon the one most wronged by it.

debates.question: Who is the angel of the LORD?

views.label: A created angel speaking for God
views.case: The word mal'akh means messenger, and ancient messengers often spoke in the first person for their master. On this view the angel speaks God's words with God's authority, which is why Hagar addresses the LORD through him, without being God Himself.

views.label: A self revelation of God, often understood as the Son before the incarnation
views.case: The angel says 'I will greatly multiply your offspring,' verse 10, a promise only God can make, and the narrator says Hagar 'gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her,' verse 13. Elsewhere those who meet the angel conclude they have seen God, Judges 13:22. Many church fathers and later interpreters saw here an appearance of the Son, who alone makes the Father known, John 1:18.

debates.bearing: The text itself identifies the angel closely with the LORD while distinguishing him in title, a tension it does not resolve. Whatever the precise identity, Hagar knew she had met God, and the chapter's theology rests on that: God Himself came to find her.

study.originalLanguages:
Sarai's reason in verse 2, 'perhaps I can build a family by her,' is literally 'perhaps I will be built from her,' ibbaneh, from banah, to build. The verb sounds like ben, son, and the wordplay is deliberate: to have a son is to be built up. Rachel uses exactly the same phrase when she gives Bilhah to Jacob, Genesis 30:3.

Hagar is a shiphchah, a maidservant, usually a woman who served her mistress personally. In Genesis 21:10 Sarah will call her an amah, 'slave woman,' a word that can carry more contempt. The shift in label tracks the shift in Hagar's standing in the household.

Verse 4 says Hagar 'began to despise her mistress,' literally that her mistress became light or slight in her eyes. The verb is qalal, to be light or trivial, and in another stem to curse. It is the verb in Genesis 12:3, 'those who curse you.' The very root God used for those who would treat Abram's family with contempt surfaces inside the family itself.

Sarai's protest in verse 5, 'May the wrong done to me be upon you,' uses chamas, violence or injustice, the word for the violence that filled the earth before the flood, Genesis 6:11. She speaks of her grievance in the strongest terms.

The root anah, to afflict, humble or oppress, runs through the chapter. Sarai 'treated Hagar so harshly' in verse 6 with the intensive form of anah. The angel says 'submit to her authority' in verse 9 with the reflexive form, literally 'humble yourself.' And in verse 11 the LORD 'has heard your cry of affliction,' oni, the noun from the same root. God does not deny the affliction; He names it and hears it. The same root describes Egypt's treatment of Israel, Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 1:11-12.

The son's name is Yishmael, 'God hears,' as the BSB footnote explains. The divine name inside it is El, the common word for God, while the angel's explanation uses the covenant name: 'for the LORD has heard.'

'A wild donkey of a man,' pere adam, uses the word for the onager of the steppe, Job 39:5. The last line of verse 12, 'he will live in hostility toward all his brothers,' is literally 'he will dwell over against the face of all his brothers,' al penei. The phrase can mean in defiance of, or simply to the east of, or alongside, and translations differ.

Verse 13 is one of the hardest lines in Genesis to translate. Hagar calls God El Roi, 'the God of seeing' or 'the God who sees me,' and then says something like 'Have I truly seen here the One who sees me?' The well's name, Beer-lahai-roi, the BSB notes, means 'well of the Living One who sees me.' The point survives every rendering: the seeing God has been seen, and the one who was overlooked has been looked upon.

typology.type: The angel of the LORD who seeks and finds the runaway
typology.fulfillment: The angel 'found' Hagar by a spring in the wilderness, called her by name and asked where she had come from and where she was going. Jesus describes His own mission in these terms: 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. In the angel, God speaks through a messenger who is closely identified with Him; in Christ, God Himself takes flesh and comes near, John 1:14. The escalation lies in the cost. The angel came with a word; Christ came to give His life for those He sought.

typology.type: The God who meets a woman at a wilderness spring
typology.fulfillment: Hagar, an outsider in shame and flight, is met by God at a spring and goes away having seen Him. Jesus, 'weary from His journey,' sits at Jacob's well and speaks to a Samaritan woman, an outsider with her own shame, John 4:6-7, and reveals Himself to her as the Messiah. The correspondence is one of pattern rather than prediction; John does not cite Genesis 16. Yet the resemblance is striking, and Christ goes further, offering not water from a well but living water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life.

typology.type: Ishmael, the son born by human effort
typology.fulfillment: Paul uses the contrast between Ishmael and Isaac directly: one was 'born according to the flesh,' the other 'born through the promise,' Galatians 4:23. Ishmael stands for every attempt to gain the inheritance by human means, including law keeping, while Isaac stands for the children God gives by His Spirit. Believers are 'like Isaac, children of promise,' Galatians 4:28. The type is negative in its main force, but the chapter itself guards against contempt for Ishmael, since God blesses him, hears him and makes him a great nation, Genesis 17:20.

typology.type: God hearing the affliction of an Egyptian slave
typology.fulfillment: God hears the cry of a foreign slave woman and gives her a future. The same God later hears Israel's cry under Egyptian slavery, Exodus 3:7, and in Christ He extends that mercy to all nations. Gentiles who were 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' are 'brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:12-13. Hagar received a promise of many descendants but not the covenant line; in Christ outsiders are brought fully into the family of Abraham, Galatians 3:29.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the figure of the angel of the LORD. He finds Hagar, speaks with God's authority, promises what only God can promise, and is recognised as God by the one he meets. The New Testament does not name this angel, and the reading needs care, but the pattern prepares for the Son, who is Himself God and 'has made Him known,' John 1:18. Isaiah 63:9 says of God's dealings with Israel, 'In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them.' In Jesus the God who came to Hagar comes to stay, and the one who sees is seen in a human face.

It leads to Christ through His way with the overlooked. Hagar is an Egyptian, a slave, a woman, pregnant and in flight, used by others and called by no name. Jesus consistently goes to people like her: the Samaritan woman at the well, John 4:7, the woman who touched His cloak, the tax collectors and outcasts. He does for them what the angel did for Hagar. He calls them by name, asks questions that let them speak, and gives them a future. 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened,' He says, 'and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28.

It leads to Christ by contrast in Paul's reading. Galatians 4:21-31 uses Hagar and Ishmael to represent birth 'according to the flesh' and slavery, and Sarah and Isaac to represent birth 'through the promise' and freedom. Paul applies it to Gentile believers being pressed to take on the law. In Christ believers are 'children of promise,' Galatians 4:28, born by the Spirit, not by human effort. The chapter's scheme to produce an heir by human means is the opposite of the gospel, in which God gives the heir and the inheritance freely.

It leads to Christ as the true Son of promise. The chapter makes readers wait. Ishmael is not the heir, and the one who will be comes later by God's power alone. That waiting points beyond Isaac to Christ, the Seed to whom the promises were made, Galatians 3:16, conceived by the Spirit when human means were impossible, Luke 1:35.

Finally, Hebrews says Christ is a high priest 'able to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15. The God who sees the afflicted has, in Jesus, known affliction from the inside.
study.god:
The chapter is one of the Bible's clearest portraits of the God who sees and hears. Hagar's name for Him, El Roi, is a confession arrived at in the wilderness, and her son's name, Ishmael, is God's own testimony: He hears. Scripture's later language of God's watchful care grows from this root. 'The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry,' Psalm 34:15, and God tells Moses, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people... I have heard them crying out,' Exodus 3:7.

God seeks. The angel 'found' Hagar, verse 7, which implies he came looking. She was running from the household of promise, away from Canaan, toward Egypt. God did not wait for her to return before He met her. Like the question in the garden, 'Where are you?' Genesis 3:9, His questions to her, 'where have you come from, and where are you going?', are not requests for information but invitations to speak.

God is just, and His justice includes the lowly. He does not endorse the scheme or excuse Sarai's harshness. He names Hagar's suffering as affliction, verse 11, and hears it. At the same time He does not simply side with her against the household. He sends her back with a promise, holding together the good of the whole family and the good of the one wronged within it.

God is faithful to His word beyond the chosen line. Ishmael is not the child of the covenant, yet God promises him countless descendants, verse 10, and later confirms, 'I will surely bless him,' Genesis 17:20. His care is not limited to those through whom He works redemption; He is, as Psalm 145:9 says, 'good to all.'

God is also patient with His people's failures. The household of promise has made a mess of the promise, yet God does not withdraw it. The next chapter renews the covenant in even fuller terms.

For worship, the chapter invites a response like Hagar's. Those who feel unseen and unheard may say with her, 'You are the God who sees me,' and find, as she did, that being seen by God is a mercy, not a threat.

crossReferences.note: The woman took the fruit and gave it to her husband. Genesis 16:3 uses the same pattern, Sarai took Hagar and gave her to Abram, and 16:2 echoes 3:17, Abram listened to the voice of his wife. The narrator presents the scheme as a small fall inside the family of promise.

God had just promised that 'one who comes from your own body will be your heir.' Genesis 16 is the attempt to secure that heir through Hagar. The promise was true, but it said nothing about Hagar, and the chapter shows what happens when a promise is filled in with human plans.

Abraham prays, 'O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!' God insists that Sarah will bear the covenant heir but answers, 'As for Ishmael, I have heard you,' a play on his name, and promises to bless him with twelve rulers and a great nation, fulfilling 16:10.

Hagar and Ishmael are sent into the wilderness, the water runs out, and she weeps. God hears the voice of the boy, the angel of God calls to Hagar, and God opens her eyes to see a well. The hearing and seeing of Genesis 16 are repeated at her second crisis.

The account of Ishmael's line lists twelve princes of tribes, settled from Havilah to Shur, and ends with 'they lived in hostility toward all their brothers,' echoing 16:12. The promise of countless descendants in 16:10 was kept, just as the angel said.

At the burning bush the LORD says, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out.' The same seeing, hearing and affliction that marked God's mercy to an Egyptian slave in Genesis 16 now marks His mercy to Hebrew slaves in Egypt.

Hannah, barren and provoked by a rival wife, prays that the LORD will 'look upon the affliction of Your maidservant.' Her situation mirrors Sarai's household from the other side, and her prayer uses the same words of seeing and affliction that Hagar experienced at the well.

When Manoah realises he has met the angel of the LORD, he says, 'We are going to die, for we have seen God!' Like Hagar in Genesis 16:13, those who meet the angel conclude they have seen God Himself, and like her they live.

Paul uses Hagar and Sarah as illustrations of two covenants, one bearing children into slavery and one bearing children of promise. Ishmael was born 'according to the flesh,' Isaac 'through the promise.' He urges Gentile believers not to seek the inheritance through law keeping.

'The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry.' The psalm puts into general form what Hagar learned personally, that God is El Roi, the God who sees, and that He hears the cry of the afflicted, as the name Ishmael declares.

'The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.' The angel of the LORD found Hagar in the wilderness, running away with nowhere to go. Jesus describes His own mission in the same terms, seeking out those who have wandered and giving them a place and a future.

Isaiah foresees 'all the flocks of Kedar' and 'the rams of Nebaioth' coming to God's altar with acceptance. Kedar and Nebaioth are Ishmael's sons, Genesis 25:13. The descendants of the wilderness son are pictured joining the worship of Zion, a hope that reaches its fulfilment in the gospel.

study.oneStory:
The first chapters of Genesis show a pattern that keeps repeating: people seizing what God intends to give, and others being harmed. In Eden the woman took and gave, and the man listened to her voice. Genesis 16 repeats that pattern inside the family God chose to undo the damage of Eden. The household of promise, instead of bringing blessing to the nations, brings affliction to an Egyptian slave.

That is the problem the chapter shows: even the chosen family cannot secure the promise by its own means, and its efforts create new victims. But the chapter also shows the answer. God comes into the wilderness, finds the one who has been wronged, hears her affliction and gives her a future. The blessing of Genesis 12:3 reaches, in a partial way, an outsider at the very moment the family of promise has failed her.

The chapter sets up what follows. The true heir will come by God's power alone, in Genesis 21, when Sarah is past the age of childbearing. Ishmael will be blessed but not chosen, and his line will run alongside Israel's as a separate people. The seeing and hearing God of Genesis 16 will see and hear Israel in Egypt, Exodus 3:7, and deliver them in the exodus.

The story continues to Christ. He is the Son of promise born by God's power, Luke 1:35, and He comes seeking the lost, the outcast and the foreigner. In Him the division between the son of the slave and the son of the free is overcome, not by denying the difference but by making all who believe children of promise, Galatians 4:28. The Gentiles who were far off are brought near, Ephesians 2:13, and Isaiah's vision of Kedar and Nebaioth at God's altar, Isaiah 60:7, begins to come true.

The story ends in a new creation where God 'will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4. No one will be unnamed, unseen or unheard. The God who saw Hagar at the well will be seen face to face by a people from every nation, Revelation 7:9, and all of them will say what she said first: You are the God who sees me.

quiz.q: Why did Sarai give Hagar to Abram?

options.text: Because she was barren and tried to secure the promised child by her own means.
options.note: Impatient with waiting, she used a customary but ultimately grievous scheme.

options.text: Because God had commanded her to do so.
options.note: It followed the custom of the day, but God never commanded it; the plan was her own.

options.text: Because Hagar asked to bear Abram's child.
options.note: Hagar was given as a servant with no say; the initiative was Sarai's.

options.text: Because Abram had rejected God's promise entirely.
options.note: Abram still held the promise; the failure was in seizing it by human means.

quiz.q: What name did Hagar give to the LORD, and why?

options.text: The God who sees me, because He noticed her in her lowest moment.
options.note: El-Roi expresses her wonder at being seen by God.

options.text: The God who provides, because He gave her water.
options.note: That naming belongs to a later scene; here the focus is on being seen.

options.text: The God of Abram, because she now served his household.
options.note: Her name for God is deeply personal, not merely borrowed from Abram.

options.text: The God who judges, because He condemned Sarai.
options.note: The name centers on God's tender attention, not on judgment.

quiz.q: What does the name Ishmael mean, and what does it testify?

options.text: God hears, testifying that the LORD heard Hagar's affliction.
options.note: The name memorializes God's attention to a mistreated slave woman.

options.text: God sees, testifying that the LORD watched over Abram.
options.note: Seeing is the theme of El-Roi; Ishmael specifically means God hears.

options.text: God laughs, testifying to Sarai's joy.
options.note: That meaning belongs to Isaac, not Ishmael.

options.text: God forgets, testifying that Hagar was abandoned.
options.note: The opposite is true; God hears and remembers her.

quiz.q: How does the angel of the LORD respond to Hagar in the desert?

options.text: He finds her, questions her gently, and gives her a promise for her son.
options.note: God pursues the runaway with care and a future.

options.text: He condemns her for fleeing and sends her away for good.
options.note: He does tell her to return, but with a promise, not condemnation.

options.text: He ignores her because she is a foreign slave.
options.note: The whole point is that God does not overlook her.

options.text: He tells her the promise is only for Sarai.
options.note: God gives Hagar her own promise of numerous offspring.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use the figure of Hagar?

options.text: Paul reads Hagar and Sarah as two covenants, slavery and the freedom of promise.
options.note: Galatians 4 develops the allegory, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: Paul presents Hagar as the model of saving faith.
options.note: Hagar receives real mercy, but Paul's allegory casts her as the covenant of slavery.

options.text: Hagar is never mentioned again in Scripture.
options.note: She appears again in Genesis 21 and in Galatians 4.

options.text: Hagar is condemned as an enemy of God.
options.note: God shows her compassion; she is used as a picture, not condemned as a person.

questions: Sarai grew tired of waiting and took a shortcut to God's promise. Where are you tempted to force an outcome rather than trust God's timing?
The scheme brought jealousy and cruelty into the home. Have you seen how trying to control an outcome can damage the people around you?
Hagar called God 'the God who sees me.' When have you felt overlooked, and what would it mean to know that God sees you right now?
God met a foreign, mistreated slave with tenderness and a promise. Who are the overlooked people around you that God is calling you to notice?
The name Ishmael means 'God hears.' What affliction do you need to bring to God this week, trusting that He hears your cry?

translationNotes.note: Angel may also be rendered Angel with a capital, and the corresponding pronouns capitalized, since the messenger speaks and is addressed as the LORD Himself.
The Hebrew behind the God who sees me is El-Roi; the verse contains a play on seeing and being seen that is difficult to render smoothly in English.
Beer-lahai-roi means well of the Living One who sees me, tying the place forever to Hagar's confession.
